content: Exercise interventions have been shown to improve aerobic fitness, muscular strength, physical functioning, quality of life (QoL), and self-efficacy in individuals. At least one study demonstrated that exercise interventions led to an increase in CD4+ cell counts and a reduction in HIV RNA viral load. Another study revealed that HIV-specific biomarkers remained stable in the exercise group, whereas they significantly worsened in the non-exercise group. Despite these well-documented benefits, exercise programs have not been widely adopted or recognized as viable therapeutic options for people living with HIV (PLWH). Understanding the potential health benefits of increased physical activity is crucial for better recommending exercise programs. However, exercise prescriptions must be carefully tailored to each individual. Further research is needed to evaluate the efficacy and effectiveness of various exercise training regimens for PLWH. From 1996 to 2015, studies addressed outcomes such as health-related quality of life (HRQoL), anxiety and depression, fitness and functional capacity, and virological markers like viral load and CD4+ counts. For example, a systematic review by Lofgren et al. (2018) focused on depression interventions for HIV-infected adults in Africa. The review identified 18 studies, with six of seven feasibility studies and all seven acceptability studies yielding positive results. Psychotherapy interventions showed a 73% relative decrease in depressive symptoms compared to a 39% decrease in controls. Task-shifting psychotherapy interventions resulted in a 47% decrease compared to 34% in controls. Antidepressant interventions demonstrated a 79% decrease in depressive symptoms, while task-shifting antidepressant treatments showed an 82% decrease compared to 65% in controls. Exercise interventions led to a 66% reduction in depressive symptoms compared to 49% in controls. One trial on minocycline showed no statistically significant results. Other psychosocial interventions resulted in a 44% decrease in depressive symptoms compared to 21% in controls. These findings underscore the need for large, randomized trials to establish efficacy and implementation strategies. Another systematic review by Leyes et al. (2008) examined the effects of diet, nutritional support, and exercise on body composition and metabolic complications in HIV-infected patients receiving combination antiretroviral therapy (cART). The review highlighted that cART improves HIV prognosis but is associated with body composition changes and metabolic alterations, collectively termed lipodystrophy syndrome. Nutritional status may influence these changes. Resistance exercise, with or without an aerobic component, was found to increase lean body mass and improve insulin resistance. Low-fat diets or exercise can reduce fat mass but should be used cautiously in individuals with lipoatrophy. Nutritional support and exercise resulted in modest but significant body composition changes and can serve as complementary interventions. However, further research is needed to explore nutritional interventions in HIV-infected patients on cART. In summary, while exercise and nutritional interventions show promise in improving physical and mental health outcomes in various populations, including those with HIV, diabetes, and cardiovascular conditions, more robust and large-scale studies are required to confirm their efficacy and optimize their implementation.
